source.title: How Far Do Auto-Interpretation Labels Generalize: A Controlled Study Across Languages, Scripts, and Rewordings

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether feature labels predict firing on equivalent content in other languages and scripts, and finds substantial miss rates, especially for Serbian and deeper layers. It challenges the generalization of labels, not the claim about neuron-pole job counts directly.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates sparse-autoencoder features, not individual neurons or neuron poles. Its main label evaluation measures whether a content-labeled feature fires on the same content in alternative language/script renderings. It does not test the claimed Qwen3-32B percentages, scale to trillion-parameter models, InceptionV1 examples, or attribution graphs. Feature-set Jaccard results are included as findings about the subject but do not directly test a listed claim version. Label-pool selection and classifier discard rates are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study scores auto-interpretation labels of Gemma Scope 2 sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, not individual neurons or neuron poles. Every version names neurons: their job shares (V1–V2), canonical neurons (V3), neuron interpretability with better tools (V4), neurons as circuit units (V5), or explanations of neurons (V6–V7). SAE features are a trained replacement basis, the very thing the essay argues against needing, so they are a different unit of analysis. Its miss-rate and inspection results are close in spirit to V6, explanations from activating examples failing elsewhere, but they measure a related construct. They are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests. The study cites Bills et al. (an original source) only as the origin of auto-interpretation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. To add: the authors say labels are locally accurate on their top-activating examples but still fail to predict firing on equivalent renderings. They read the labels as claims about a feature's behavior on its best-represented inputs, not guarantees about the concept. The failures are graded in line with estimated training-data coverage.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Gemma Scope SAE features and Neuronpedia auto-interpretation labels, then evaluates feature firing on matched translations, transliterations, paraphrases, and random partners. This is not the original neuron-pole audit or an activation-explanation score.
record.method_sensitivity: Miss rates and Serbian Cyrillic/Latin asymmetry vary by network layer; the gap grows at greater depth. The study reports similar patterns from Claude Sonnet and Gemini Flash Lite, and qualitative replication of label failures across Gemma-3-1B, Gemma-3-12B, and Gemma-3-27B.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features selected because they fire on both the English and Russian versions of a sentence, and labelled for content by Neuronpedia, fail to fire on the same content in other renderings. Within-language miss rates are 7–17%. Serbian miss rates reach 30.1% (Serbian average, layer 53) and 34.6% (Serbian Cyrillic) in Gemma-3-27B, and up to 58% in Gemma-3-1B. Serbian Cyrillic is missed more than Serbian Latin (up to 1.35x), with the gap growing with depth. The pattern holds with both labelers (Claude Sonnet, Gemini Flash Lite).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Auto-interpretation labels of SAE features fail to predict the features' firing on equivalent content in less-represented languages and scripts, increasingly so with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: In a manual check of 60 missed units, labels described the top-activating examples at least partly in 92% of cases. Yet the labelled concept was present in the missed sentence in only 58% (42% strictly), so the features fire on inputs outside their label. This is an SAE-feature analogue of V6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An SAE-feature label accurate on its top-activating examples does not reliably describe where the feature fires on other inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Active SAE-feature sets overlap across changes of script (0.73), language (0.50) and wording (0.63). Meaning-only overlap averages 0.39 against a 0.13 random baseline, peaking at 0.57.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature sets in multilingual LMs retain substantial cross-lingual semantic overlap.

record.problems: The evaluation uses 300 sentences and only three languages; Serbian is closely related to Russian. Label-failure evaluation is reported for Gemma models, not other model families or labeling pipelines. Neuronpedia labels are mutable, though the authors say cached bundles are released. Manual inspection of missed features used one annotator.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted the separate Serbian paraphrase miss-rate conditions, Russian and English random-partner controls, Gemini random-partner controls, and other reported auxiliary breakdowns. Relevant additional results appear in Tables 22–29 and Appendix E; the retained rows include the main labeler/model/layer comparisons, Serbian original-script conditions, and representative random controls.

untested.parts: No neuron-pole audit and no Qwen3-32B job shares.
No neuron interpretability shares across dense or mixture-of-experts models, nor at trillion-parameter scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No comparison of neuron interpretability across architectures, regularization or tools.
No attribution graphs built from neurons.
Explanations of individual neurons are not evaluated; only SAE-feature labels are.
No simulation-based explanation scores for neurons.

missing.what: Human verification of missed features: label accurate on top-activating examples 92% (Yes or Partly); concept present in the missed sentence 58% (Yes or Partly) / 42% (strict).
Serbian paraphrase miss rates and the unfiltered-pool ratios (Table 28).
Llama-3.1-8B Leg 1 replication: script Jaccard mean 0.48.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all miss-rate rows to V6 and labelled them supports. That link is rejected: the study's unit is the SAE feature, not the neuron, and V6 targets explanations of neurons. If the curators decide SAE-feature labels count for V6, then rows R1–R48 and Table 30 would support V6, with limits_scope by layer (smaller gaps at early layers, e.g. Cyrillic/Latin 1.02x at layer 16 in 27B). The study selects features that fire on English and Russian, so cross-language miss magnitudes are upper bounds, as the authors note.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of neuron poles or estimates of their number of jobs.
Does not measure neuron interpretability shares across dense and mixture-of-experts models or up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures, regularization, or tool quality.
No attribution-graph reconstruction or test of neurons as circuit units.

Tests Neuronpedia SAE-feature labels against firing on equivalent content in alternative languages and scripts; it does not test explanations of individual neurons or the full range of inputs that could contradict an explanation.
Does not apply an explanation-quality score or threshold to determine the share of explanations that score well; its miss rates are not the stated minority-good-score outcome.

reader_labels.condition: Gemma-3-27B, both labelers, layers 16, 31, 40, and 53; Gemma-3-1B and Gemma-3-12B scale replications
reader_labels.reason: Content-labeled feature miss rates are nonzero within languages and generally higher on Serbian; the Serbian Cyrillic disadvantage grows with depth in the main model and is also reported in scale replications (R1–R48).
